notes:
I found good material for all three verses. I didn't find anything on this psalm from the Lutheran, Orthodox, Pentecostal-denomination (ag.org, pneumareview.com) or Wesleyan seminary sites, nor any prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on it, so those parts are left out. A few traditions are covered by older commentators on biblehub and studylight instead: Methodists Adam Clarke and Joseph Benson, Lutheran scholars Keil and Delitzsch, Reformed Calvin and Matthew Henry, and Baptist Spurgeon.

---

## Introduction and setting

- **When David wrote it.** Guzik gives two possible occasions. One is when Saul was hunting David, either when Saul hunted him or when Michal mocked him for dancing before the ark (2 Sam 6:16–23). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-131/
- **Captivity view.** Clarke reports that some see David defending himself against Saul's courtiers. Others think the Psalm was made during the captivity, describing how the captives behaved under their oppressors. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nkj/psalms/131-1.html
- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran scholarship).** The title links the psalm to David because it echoes his answer to Michal (2 Sam 6:21). They say the poet holds up David's character as a mirror to the Israel of the period after the Exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/131-3.htm
- **Type of psalm.** Constable calls it an individual psalm of confidence that became a psalm of ascent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/131-3.html
- **Spurgeon's summary**, quoted by Guzik: short to read… actually "one of the shortest Psalms to read, but one of the longest to learn." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-131/

## v. 1: "My heart is not proud…"

**Traditional reading**
- **Guzik:** David rejects three things: pride ("heart"), arrogance ("eyes," looking down on others) and selfish ambition ("great matters"). He links this to "God resists the proud" (Prov 3:34; James 4:6). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-131/
- **Guzik on "things too lofty":** this can also mean prideful mental pursuits, where we demand to know what God hasn't revealed. That was Job's sin, and David followed Deut 29:29. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-131/
- **Piper (Baptist):** David kills pride at three levels: feeling (heart), appearance (eyes) and action ("walk in"). Piper names two kinds of pride, the "pride of having" and the "pride of wanting," and warns that pride often shows up in those who crave attention, not just in the arrogant. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/join-me-in-soul-satisfaction-in-god
- **Keil & Delitzsch** read the same three parts: pride of the soul, pride of countenance, and pride of endeavour and mode of action. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/131-3.htm
- **Clarke (Methodist):** David neither looks up wanting others' rank nor look down with contempt to the meanness or poverty of those below me. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/131-1.html
- **Matthew Henry:** David didn't pursue "nice speculation" or try to be wise beyond what is written. To know God and our duty is learning sufficiently high for us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/131-1.html
- **Barnes:** David is denying a false charge of ambition: What I have said was not the result of ambition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/131-1.html
- **Constable:** Pride is essentially a belief that one does not need God but is self-sufficient. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/131-1.html
- **Coffman:** the verse doesn't forbid research into mysteries. It teaches that some things lie beyond human limits. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/131-1.html
- **Keller (TGC):** the reason God's actions are often opaque is not because we are wise and he is foolish, but because he is too "great" and "wonderful" for us. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/contentment/
- **Calvin (Reformed):** with a clear call from God, nothing is "too great" for the obedient. But those driven by ambition will soon lose themselves in a labyrinth of perplexity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/131-1.html

## v. 2: "Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul…"

**Traditional reading**
- **"Surely" may be an oath.** Ellicott says the Hebrew literally reads "if not," a form commonly used to express strong asseveration after an oath. https://biblehub.com/psalms/131-2.htm Gill cites Kimchi and Aben Ezra for the same oath reading. Calvin translates it "If I have not set…" https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/131-2.html
- **"Stilled."** Barnes says the word means to make level or smooth, here used for calming the mind; smoothing down its roughnesses; keeping it tranquil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/131-2.htm
- **Weaned, not nursing.** Guzik: the nursing child wants food, but a weaned child embraces his mother out of a desire for love, closeness, and companionship. The child learns that being denied a gift isn't being denied the mother. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-131/ Keller makes the same point: a weaned child is satisfied just with mother herself, with her very presence. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/contentment/
- **The struggle behind the calm.** Ellicott says the picture comes from a baby's first real sorrow. He moans, and frets, and sobs, but at last is quieted by the love which is powerful to soothe, even when it must deny. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/131-2.htm Coffman: this calm was won by mastering what disturbed him, not inborn. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-131.html
- **Kidner vs. the RSV.** Coffman, following Kidner, says the RSV ("a child quieted at its mother's breast") blunts the point. It is a "weaned child" not a nursing child that is mentioned here. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-131.html
- **Matthew Henry:** Providence puts wormwood upon the breast, and that helps to wean us. When our condition is not to our mind we must bring our mind to our condition. He also says David didn't grasp at the crown before God's time. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_131.cfm
- **Gill:** David was weaned from the world's riches and honours, and from his own righteousness, and from all dependence on it. He had no more craving for the kingdom than a weaned child for the breast. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/131-2.htm
- **Calvin:** David put aside the anxieties of ambition and was willing to be satisfied with small things. The comparison isn't with a suckling, because a suckling still longs for the breast. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/131-2.html
- **Cambridge Bible (on Biblehub):** the point isn't the child's helplessness, but its contentment in spite of the loss of what once seemed indispensable. Children in the East were sometimes nursed until about age three. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/131-2.htm
- **Benson (Methodist):** David restrained and subdued all such sinful motions or dispositions. He relied wholly on God's providence, like an infant on its mother. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/131-2.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** the soul, which is by nature restless and craving, is stilled. It is satisfied in fellowship with God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/131-3.htm
- **God pictured as a mother.** Guzik calls this one of the few passages that picture God in some way as a mother, alongside Isa 49:15 and 66:13. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-131/

**Where teachers put the emphasis differently: who quiets the soul?**
This is a difference of emphasis between teachers, not a formal split between denominations.
- **Guzik (Enduring Word, listed by you under Pentecostal/charismatic) stresses human choice.** The calm was ultimately God's work, but God didn't do this *for* him; God used the operation of David's choice. We must choose to calm and quiet our soul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-131/
- **Piper (Reformed Baptist) stresses God as the source.** David doesn't mean he produced his own calm: The weaned child isn't curled up in front of a mirror. Piper sums it up as "Not 'I have produced it,' but 'I have pursued it.'" https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/join-me-in-soul-satisfaction-in-god
- **Spurgeon (Baptist) stresses grace.** We are clamorous, uneasy, petulant; and nothing but grace can make us quiet under afflictions, irritations, and disappointments. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps131.cfm
- **Clarke and Benson (Methodist)** present it as David's own self-restraint (see Benson above).

**Other views**
- **NET Bible translation.** It renders the verse "like a young child carried by its mother; I am content like the young child I carry." This seems to make the speaker the one carrying the child. I could only see the translation, not the NET notes explaining it. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=131
- **Augustine (Catholic, newadvent).**
  - He hears the psalm as the voice of the whole body of Christ.
  - His Latin text reads the verse as a self-curse: if I was proud, may my reward be like a child taken from the breast too soon.
  - He warns against being weaned "before the time," as he says heretics were. Believers should take the milk of faith in Christ until they can handle solid food.
  - https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801131.htm
- **Aquinas (Catholic).** He quotes a gloss on this verse (Ps 130:2 in Latin numbering). It compares the newly baptized to infants fed on milk until Pentecost, then "weaned" at confirmation into harder disciplines. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3189.htm

## v. 3: "O Israel, put your hope in the LORD…"

**Traditional reading**
- **Guzik:** the lesson can only be lived by hoping in the LORD and in nothing else. Hope should begin "now" and continue forever. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-131/
- **Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik)** on the shift to the whole people: Weaning takes the child out of a temporary condition into a state in which he will continue for the rest of his life. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-131/
- **Piper:** verse 3 shows that verse 2's calm is contentment in God. David invites Israel to join him and seek their soul's satisfaction in God. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/join-me-in-soul-satisfaction-in-god
- **Henry and Gill:** David's supporters may have been impatient to put him on the throne, so he tells them to wait for God's timing. Gill compares 1 Sam 24:7. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/131-3.html; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/131-3.htm
- **Calvin:** the call matters to the church because it shows David reigned by God's appointment. Our hope is of the right kind when we cherish humble and sober views of ourselves. https://ccel.org/study/Ps_131
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** here the psalm moves from one person to the whole congregation. Israel is to renounce all self-boasting and all self-activity, and to wait in lowliness and quietness upon its God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/131-3.htm
- **Clarke (Methodist):** don't just assume troubles will wear out on their own. Look to God, who is wise to plan, good to purpose and strong to carry it out. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/131-3.html
- **Utley (bible.org):** the word "hope" is the same one used in 130:5–7. It carries the idea of patient trust, and the psalmist uses his own example to call Israel to it. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-131
- **Barnes** applies the verse to Christ, the greater Son of David, who as a twelve-year-old amazed the teachers in the temple (Luke 2:47). He sees in it modesty joined with unusual gifts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/131-3.htm
- **Kidner (quoted by Guzik):** the verse moves us from looking at David to following him and his greater Son, being weaned onto "solid fare" (John 4:34). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-131/

**Other views**
- **Augustine (Catholic):** Until we arrive at eternity, let us trust in the Lord God; because when we have reached eternity, there will be no longer hope, but the thing itself will be ours. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801131.htm
